stem: Your extraction agent calls extract_invoice with period_start values such as "March 3 2026" and "03/03/26". The tool requires ISO 8601 dates and rejects 23% of calls with a validation error, each costing an extra round trip. Its description reads "Extracts invoice fields for a billing period." What is the most effective fix?

options.text: Expand the description to state that period_start and period_end must be ISO 8601 dates, with an example call showing the format.
Add a PostToolUse hook that rewrites date arguments into ISO 8601 before the tool runs, so malformed dates never reach it.
Loosen the tool to accept any date string and let the server parse whatever format the model happens to send.
Add four few-shot examples to the system prompt showing correctly formatted extract_invoice calls for different billing periods.

explanation: Input formats belong in the tool description, which is where the model looks before it builds the arguments. Naming the format and showing one example removes the cause of the rejected calls.

why.B: PostToolUse intercepts tool results, not outgoing arguments, and hiding the format in a hook leaves the description that caused the errors unchanged.
why.C: Accepting any string trades a visible validation error for a silent one, since 03/03/26 is ambiguous and a wrong reading dates the invoice incorrectly.
why.D: Few-shot examples pay tokens on every request to compensate for input format detail that belongs in the tool description.

stem: You add find_symbol_definition to a code exploration agent that already has search_repository ("Searches the repository and returns matching locations"). Across 1,200 sessions the new tool was called 3 times while search_repository absorbed the symbol lookups. The new tool's description names its inputs, outputs and boundaries. What is the most effective fix?

options.text: Add few-shot examples to the system prompt showing symbol lookups routed to find_symbol_definition and text searches to search_repository.
Remove search_repository from the agent so symbol lookups have only one tool left that they can land on.
Narrow search_repository's description to text search, and state in both descriptions which requests belong to the other tool.
Rename find_symbol_definition to search_symbols so its name matches the phrasing developers use in their requests.

explanation: Selection is driven by descriptions, and the overlap lives in the older tool's broad wording. A boundary written on only one side cannot help while the other tool still claims to search the repository generally.

why.A: Examples paper over an overlap that still exists in the descriptions, and pay for it in tokens on every request.
why.B: Drops a capability the agent still needs for text searches, and the overlap returns with the next tool that mentions searching.
why.D: A new name does not tell the model what the tool does differently, so the broader description keeps absorbing the requests.

stem: Your always-loaded project instructions include the line "Always confirm the current database schema before writing any code." Since it was added, the agent opens nearly every session with a describe_schema call, including CSS-only and documentation tasks, costing about 4,000 tokens and a round trip each time. The tool descriptions are detailed and accurate. What should you change?

options.text: Shorten describe_schema's description so it competes less strongly for requests that have nothing to do with the database.
Rewrite the instruction to name its condition, so the schema check applies only before code that reads or writes the database.
Move describe_schema to a user-scoped MCP server so it loads only for the developers who work on data access code.
Add a hook that blocks describe_schema unless the session has already opened a file under the data access directory.

explanation: Keyword-sensitive instruction wording overrides well written tool descriptions. The instruction says any code, so the agent obeys it literally, and scoping that sentence to the case it was written for is the smallest fix.

why.A: The description is not what drives the call. Weakening a good description also degrades the cases where the tool is genuinely needed.
why.C: Scoping changes who has the tool, not when it is called, and it takes the tool away from teammates who need it on data work.
why.D: Deterministic machinery for a wording problem, and it blocks legitimate first calls where the schema is needed before any file is opened.

stem: Your CI review agent calls get_pull_request_diff and then calls list_changed_files on 88% of runs, adding a round trip to every review, even though the diff response already contains each changed file and its status. list_changed_files is also the only source the release notes job has. The description of get_pull_request_diff reads "Fetches the diff for a pull request." What is the most effective change?

options.text: Remove list_changed_files from the review agent so the redundant second call becomes impossible to make.
Add a PostToolUse hook that drops the second response when a diff was already fetched in the same run.
Add a caching layer in front of both tools so repeated pull request lookups inside one run are served locally.
Expand the description to state what the response contains, including the list of changed files with their status.

explanation: Descriptions carry outputs as well as inputs. The agent asks for the file list because nothing tells it the diff response already holds one, so documenting the response removes the reason for the second call.

why.A: Amputates a tool other jobs use, and the agent is still unaware of what the diff returns, so it will look for the file list elsewhere.
why.B: The extra call has already been made by the time a PostToolUse hook can see it, so the round trip and its tokens are still spent.
why.C: Speculative caching hides the symptom. The agent still issues a call it does not need, because nothing tells it the data is in hand.

stem: Your document fetch tool returns errorCategory "transient" with isRetryable true for every failure. Last month 340 documents in restricted client folders returned HTTP 403, because the pipeline account has no access there. Each was retried three times and then dropped from the run with no record. What should the tool return for those 403 responses?

options.text: A transient error with isRetryable true and a longer backoff, since access to those folders can be granted at any time.
A permission error with isRetryable false and a description naming the folder and the access that is missing.
A validation error with isRetryable false, so the agent corrects the document_id argument and moves to the next document.
A success carrying an empty field set, so the batch completes and the missing documents surface as gaps downstream.

explanation: A 403 is a permission failure: not retryable, and fixable only outside the run. Categorising it that way with a readable reason stops the wasted retries and gives the operator something to act on.

why.A: A 403 will not clear on its own inside the run, so every retry is wasted and the document still disappears without explanation.
why.C: The arguments were valid. Calling this a validation error sends the agent hunting for an input bug that does not exist.
why.D: Reporting a failure as a success is the anti-pattern that produced the silent data loss in the first place.

stem: extract_tables handles multi-page scans. When 3 of 40 pages are too faint to parse, the tool returns isError true with "Extraction failed" and your pipeline discards the document. 8% of documents are lost this way, most of them with 30 or more pages that extracted cleanly. What should the tool return instead?

options.text: isError true with the numbers of the pages that failed, so the pipeline can resubmit the whole document later.
A success containing the tables that extracted, since the pages that produced nothing have nothing to report.
isError true with the parser exception for each failed page, so an engineer can diagnose the faint scans.
A success carrying the extracted tables plus a structured entry naming the pages that could not be read and why.

explanation: The call partly succeeded, so it should carry partial results together with structured detail about what failed. The pipeline keeps 37 pages of tables and routes only the unread pages for follow-up.

why.A: Marking the whole call a failure still throws away the 37 clean pages and buys a full re-run that will fail the same way.
why.B: With no record of the unread pages, nothing downstream can tell an incomplete document from a complete one.
why.C: Engineering diagnostics do not belong in the agent's context, and the call is still reported as a total failure.

stem: Your repository indexing MCP server rejects malformed queries with errorCategory validation and isRetryable false, and the human-readable field reads "Invalid input." The agent correctly stops retrying, but across 600 sessions it abandoned the task three times out of four rather than sending a corrected query. What is missing from the error response?

options.text: A retry-after value in seconds, so the agent waits for the index to settle and sends the query again.
A description naming the rejected argument and the values it will accept on a corrected call.
The validator's full output for every argument in the call, including the ones that were accepted.
isRetryable true, since a corrected query can succeed and the agent needs to be allowed to send one.

explanation: The category and the flag are already right: the identical call cannot succeed. What is missing is the readable half of the response, which is what lets the agent fix its arguments instead of giving up.

why.A: There is nothing to wait for. A validation failure is permanent for those arguments, so a delay changes nothing.
why.C: Buries the one rejected argument in output about the ones that passed, and spends context on detail the agent cannot act on.
why.D: isRetryable answers whether the identical call can succeed, and it cannot. Marking it true restarts the retries the flag exists to stop.

stem: Your extraction server exposes extract_fields(document_id, fields), and today all four outcomes below are reported the same way, so the pipeline cannot tell a failed call from a thin document. Which two should be returned with isError set to true? (Select 2)

options.text: The document is fetched and parsed, and none of the requested fields appear anywhere in it.
The document management system does not answer within the tool's 30 second timeout.
The fields array contains "vat_ratio", which is not a field this extractor knows how to produce.
The document is fetched and 6 of the 8 requested fields are found, the other 2 being absent from the source.

explanation: A timeout is a transient access failure and an unsupported field name is a validation error, so both are genuine tool failures. Empty and partial results are successful calls and must stay distinguishable from them.

why.A: A successful query with no matches. Returning it as an error sends the pipeline into retries for a document that simply lacks those fields.
why.D: A partial extraction is still a success. The absent fields belong in the result as nulls rather than in an error.

stem: Your CI agent uses lookup_flaky_tests, which searches an index built from the last 30 days of pipeline runs. Its description reads "Returns the flake history for a test" and says nothing about that window. When the agent queries a test quarantined six months ago it gets an empty result and reports the test as a new failure, which has happened on 14 pull requests this quarter. What is the most effective fix?

options.text: State the 30 day window in the description, so an empty result reads as no data rather than no flakes.
Have the tool return isError true when a test has no entries in the index, so the agent stops trusting empty results.
Extend the index to cover 12 months of pipeline runs so that quarantined tests fall inside the window.
Add a system prompt line telling the agent to treat flake history for older tests as unreliable.

explanation: Boundaries and edge cases belong in the tool description. The tool answered correctly for what it holds, and the agent misread the answer because nothing told it what the index covers.

why.B: The query succeeded and matched nothing. Reporting that as a failure hides a valid empty result behind an error the agent will retry.
why.C: Buys one wider window at real cost and leaves the same misreading waiting at 12 months, because the boundary is still undocumented.
why.D: Prompt wording competing with a description that still claims full flake history, and it gives the agent no rule for telling an old test from a new one.

stem: A community MCP server gives your codebase agent a run_shell tool that executes any command. In four incidents this quarter it ran destructive commands that discarded uncommitted work. Across 900 reviewed sessions the only commands it ever needs are the test runner, the linter and the type checker. What is the right change?

options.text: Replace run_shell with three scoped tools, run_tests, run_linter and run_type_check, that take no free-form command.
Keep run_shell and list the permitted commands in the agent's system prompt, naming the destructive ones as forbidden.
Keep run_shell and add a PostToolUse hook that restores any files a command deleted from the working tree.
Keep run_shell and require a developer to approve each command before it is allowed to execute.

explanation: Replacing a generic tool with narrowly scoped alternatives removes the capability that caused the incidents while keeping everything the agent actually uses.

why.B: Prompt rules are probabilistic, and the capability being constrained is destructive, so the residual failure rate is the whole problem.
why.C: PostToolUse runs after the command has executed. Recovery after the fact is not the same as preventing the call.
why.D: Puts a human in front of hundreds of harmless test runs to catch four incidents, stalling the agent it was meant to make useful.

stem: Your MCP server already publishes the issue catalog as a resource and it works well. The team now wants the agent to file issues too. A prototype models filing as a second resource the agent writes to, and in testing the agent has no way to learn the new issue's number, or that its priority value was rejected. How should filing be exposed?

options.text: As a resource the agent writes to, plus a second resource it reads afterwards to see what the write did.
As a resource, keeping every issue operation on one mechanism so the interface stays consistent.
As a create_issue tool, since tools take actions and return results while resources expose content.
As a resource for filing plus a tool that reports whether the last write succeeded.

explanation: Resources expose content for the agent to read, and actions belong in tools. A tool call returns a result the agent can use and a structured error when input is rejected, which is exactly what the prototype could not do.

why.A: Two round trips and a race, to recover information that a tool call would have returned directly in its result.
why.B: Consistency for its own sake, at the price of an operation the agent cannot confirm, correct, or report on.
why.D: Splits one action across two mechanisms, so the agent still cannot tell which write the reported status belongs to.

stem: Your extraction service runs one agent holding 16 tools: 6 for document retrieval, 6 for field extraction across three schemas, and 4 for the human review queue. Selection errors cluster at the boundaries, with 12% of retrieval requests landing on an extraction tool and 9% of extractions calling a review queue tool. All 16 descriptions have been reviewed and are accurate and well differentiated. What is the right change?

options.text: Split the pipeline into three role-scoped agents, each holding only the tools for its own stage.
Remove the 4 review queue tools and have an operator move flagged documents into the queue by hand.
Force the retrieval tool with tool_choice on the first request for every document, then allow free selection.
Rewrite all 16 descriptions to name the pipeline stage each tool belongs to and the stages it does not serve.

explanation: The descriptions are already differentiated, so what is left is decision complexity: 16 candidates on every call. Giving each stage its own agent and its own tools removes the boundaries the errors cluster on, and no capability is lost.

why.B: Drops a capability the pipeline uses, and puts a person in the loop for routing work the agent was doing correctly most of the time.
why.C: Pins one step of three and leaves the extraction to review queue boundary untouched, which is where 9% of the errors are.
why.D: The descriptions were already reviewed and differentiated, so more wording does not shrink a 16 way choice on every call.

stem: Your CI review agent runs with Read, Write, Edit, Bash, Grep and Glob plus the eight tools from your deployment MCP server. In 9 of 210 runs it edited source files while reviewing, and in 2 runs it called trigger_deploy. The job is only supposed to read code and post findings. Which two changes fix this? (Select 2)

options.text: Restrict the review job's allowedTools to Read, Grep, Glob and the reporting tool.
Add a line to the review prompt stating that the agent must never modify files or trigger a deployment.
Detach the deployment MCP server from the review job and keep it configured only for the deploy job.
Have a reviewer inspect the working tree after each run and revert anything the agent changed.

explanation: The agent misused tools it should never have held, so the fix works on both sides of its tool set: scope the built-ins to the read-only ones the job needs, and stop attaching a deployment server to a review job.

why.B: Prompt guidance where a guarantee is required. The destructive tools stay attached, with a non-zero failure rate on every run.
why.D: Shifts the burden onto humans after the fact, and does nothing about the deployments that have already fired.

stem: Your team's shared MCP server gained a new tool, deploy_preview, at 09:30. Developers who started a session after that can call it. Three developers whose sessions have been open since 08:00 cannot, and their .mcp.json is identical to everyone else's. What explains this?

options.text: Their .mcp.json needs deploy_preview listed by name before the client will offer the tool to the model.
Tools are discovered at connection time, so a session open since 08:00 still holds the earlier list.
Tool descriptions are cached per project, and that cache is only rebuilt when the project's CLAUDE.md changes.
The new tool is user-scoped until someone adds it to the project's committed configuration.

explanation: Tools from every configured server are discovered when the client connects to it. A session that connected before the tool shipped keeps the list it was given, and a session started afterwards picks up the addition.

why.A: .mcp.json names servers, not their tools. The client asks each server what it offers, so there is no per-tool entry to add.
why.C: There is no description cache keyed to CLAUDE.md. The tool list comes from the server itself at connection time.
why.D: Scope decides who gets a server, not when its tools appear, and this server is already project-scoped for all of them.

stem: A developer asks Claude Code to raise one timeout constant in a 4,200 line configuration module. The line const REQUEST_TIMEOUT_MS = 5000; appears exactly once in the file. The agent read the whole file and wrote it back, and the diff carries the intended change plus 40 lines of incidental reformatting nobody asked for. What should it have done?

options.text: Read the file and Write it back as before, with an instruction to leave every other line untouched.
Use Bash with sed to replace 5000 wherever it appears in the module, which touches only that value.
Use Edit with the constant line as its anchor, since the anchor is unique and one line changes.
Split the module into smaller files first, so that rewriting any one of them stays safe to do.

explanation: Edit is the targeted modification tool and it needs unique anchor text, which this line supplies. Read plus Write is the fallback for when no unique anchor exists, and using it here made the agent re-emit 4,200 lines it had to reproduce exactly.

why.A: The rewrite is still 4,200 lines of reproduction, and an instruction to be careful is the thing that just failed.
why.B: 5000 appears in other settings in the module, so a blind substitution changes values the agent never looked at.
why.D: A restructuring of the codebase to make a one line change safe, when a targeted edit was available all along.

stem: A developer asks the agent to review only what changed on their feature branch. The repository holds 3,100 TypeScript files and the branch touches 11. The agent globbed for every .ts file and started reading alphabetically, filling most of the context before it reached a changed file. Which approach gets the right file set?

options.text: Glob for every .ts file, then sort the results by modification time and Read the most recently touched ones.
Grep the repository for the branch name to find the files this feature work has touched.
Read the package manifest and follow imports from the entry point until the changed modules appear.
Use Bash to ask git for the paths that differ from the merge base, then Read only those files.

explanation: Neither Grep nor Glob knows version history, so the changed file set has to come from git through Bash. Reading only those 11 files keeps the review in scope and the context small.

why.A: Modification times reflect checkouts, installs and builds, so the list has no relationship to what the branch changed.
why.B: Branch names do not appear in source files. This searches file contents for something that was never written there.
why.C: An unbounded traversal that reads the context away without ever identifying which files are new work.
